Prevention: Dendrobium orchids near these five host plant families as the midge will multiply in them: (Malvaceae)
Hibiscus, Solanaceae) tomato, eggplant, potato, (Cruciferae) white mustard cabbage, (Cucurbitaceae) bitter melon, (Oleaceae)
If grown in green house make sure the interior is midge free before planting
Monitoring: Weekly inspections of the flower buds as life cycle of the midge is 21-28 days
Look for deformed unopened flower buds and aborted bud development.
When infestation is severe, bud rot and blossom drop will occur due to secondary infections
Check deformed unopened buds for maggots.
Newly hatched maggots are white whereas more mature maggots are yellow with a tinge of pink.
Check for the adult fly which is tiny and mosquito- like.
It has large eyes and a single pair of spotted wings 1 to 2 times as long as its body.
It survives for only 4 days as an adult.
Action needs to be taken if one infested flower bud is identified.
Direct Control: Remove all dropped buds and destroy infected buds
Place infected buds in a plastic bag and seal to prevent maggots from escaping and then burn
Restrictions: Except for the adult stage, the midge is secluded in the flower bud and the soil.
Only the adult stage is vulnerable to contact and translaminar insecticides.
Ensure that appropriate personal protective equipment is used when applying agro chemicals.
Apply as a foliar spray preferably in the early evening at a rate of 2.5 grams/gal twice weekly.
Drench soil to target pupal stage
Apply as a foliar spray preferably in the early evening at a rate of ¼ teaspoon/gal twice weekly.
Drench soil to target pupal stage
